name: Tokugawa Ieyasu
info: Tokugawa Ieyasu, born Matsudaira Takechiyo in 1543, was a Japanese daimyo who seized power after the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 and founded the Tokugawa shogunate, which ruled Japan from 1603 until 1868.

facts.born: 31 January 1543, at Okazaki Castle in Mikawa Province, as Matsudaira Takechiyo; son of Matsudaira Hirotada, daimyo of Mikawa of the Matsudaira clan, and Odai no Kata
facts.died: 1 June 1616, aged 73; the cause is thought to have been cancer or syphilis, and his physician had diagnosed stomach cancer
facts.role: Daimyo of Mikawa and, from 1567, head of the Tokugawa clan; ruler of the Kantō provinces under Toyotomi Hideyoshi; one of the Council of Five Elders (1598); shōgun (1603–1605); retired shōgun, ōgosho (1605–1616)
facts.known: founding the Tokugawa shogunate; victory at the Battle of Sekigahara; making Edo, now Tokyo, the seat of power; the alliance with Oda Nobunaga; the sieges of Osaka and the end of the Toyotomi line; the Buke shohatto and the bakuhan system; the 1614 ban on Christianity

t: The son of a minor daimyo who spent his childhood as a hostage, Ieyasu built his strength over four decades as ally of Oda Nobunaga and then vassal of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, outlasting both.
His victory at Sekigahara in 1600 and appointment as shōgun in 1603 founded a government that ruled Japan until the Meiji Restoration in 1868.

He bound the daimyo to the shogunate by oaths, laws and redistributed domains, and destroyed the Toyotomi line at Osaka in 1615, a campaign in which George Sansom called him cruel, relentless and merciless.
dyk: After his defeat at Mikatagahara, Ieyasu ordered the gates of his castle left open, with torches lit and drums sounding; the Takeda generals suspected a trap and did not besiege it.
ev: Matsudaira Takechiyo, the future Ieyasu, is born at Okazaki Castle in Mikawa Province
Imagawa Yoshimoto is killed at the Battle of Okehazama; Ieyasu reclaims Okazaki Castle and then allies with Oda Nobunaga
After Nobunaga's death at Honnō-ji, Ieyasu escapes across Iga Province to Mikawa and moves into the former Takeda lands
He gives up his five provinces and moves to eight provinces in the Kantō region, making Edo his seat
The Eastern Army under Ieyasu defeats Ishida Mitsunari's Western Army at the Battle of Sekigahara
Emperor Go-Yōzei gives him the title of shōgun; he passes it to his son Hidetada in 1605
Osaka Castle falls and Toyotomi Hideyori, his mother and his infant son die, ending the Toyotomi line
Ieyasu dies at the age of 73 and is posthumously deified as Tōshō Daigongen

sections.early:
Tokugawa Ieyasu was born at Okazaki Castle on 31 January 1543, and was first named Matsudaira Takechiyo. His father, Matsudaira Hirotada, was a minor warlord of the Matsudaira clan who controlled part of Mikawa Province and a stretch of the Tōkaidō highway; his mother, Odai no Kata, was the daughter of a neighbouring samurai lord, Mizuno Tadamasa. The territory lay between stronger neighbours, the Imagawa clan of Suruga to the east and the Oda clan to the west. In the year of his birth the Matsudaira split, and when the Mizuno declared for Oda Nobuhide, Hirotada divorced Odai no Kata and sent her back to her family.

Seeking the help of Imagawa Yoshimoto, Hirotada agreed to send his heir to Sunpu as a hostage. Oda Nobuhide had the five-year-old abducted and threatened to execute him unless Hirotada broke with the Imagawa; Hirotada refused, and the boy was held for three years at the Honshōji Temple in Nagoya. Hirotada died in 1549 of unknown causes; a popular theory that he was murdered by bribed vassals is called unreliable in a study by Muraoka Mikio. In 1551, after an agreement between the Imagawa general Sessai and Oda Nobunaga, Takechiyo was taken to Sunpu, where he was treated fairly well.

He came of age in 1556, with Yoshimoto presiding, and took the name Motonobu. A year later he married Lady Tsukiyama, a relative of Yoshimoto, and became Motoyasu; their son Nobuyasu was born the next year. He fought his first battle for the Imagawa at the siege of Terabe in 1558.
sections.rise:
In 1560 Imagawa Yoshimoto invaded Oda territory with 25,000 men and was killed by Oda Nobunaga in a surprise assault at Okehazama, where Motoyasu, sent to take the fort of Marune, was not present. He marched into the abandoned Okazaki Castle, reclaimed his ancestral seat and allied with Nobunaga, at first in secret because his wife and son were hostages at Sunpu; in 1561 he openly broke with the Imagawa and exchanged captured hostages for them. In 1563 he took the name Ieyasu. He put down the Ikkō-ikki, a movement of peasants and militant monks of the Jōdo Shinshū sect, at the Battle of Azukizaka in 1564, where bullets struck but did not pierce his armour, and by 1565 was master of all Mikawa. In 1567 he adopted the family name Tokugawa.

With Takeda Shingen he divided the Imagawa lands, taking Tōtōmi and in 1570 making Hamamatsu his capital, and he fought beside Nobunaga against the Asakura and Azai. Shingen then turned on him and early in 1573 overwhelmed his army at Mikatagahara. In 1575 the Oda-Tokugawa forces, 38,000 strong, defeated Takeda Katsuyori at Nagashino, and in 1582 the Takeda were destroyed and Ieyasu received Suruga.

When Nobunaga died at Honnō-ji in 1582 Ieyasu escaped across Iga Province and then won Kai and Shinano in a three-sided war with the Hōjō and Uesugi. In 1584 he backed Oda Nobukatsu against Toyotomi Hideyoshi and beat Hideyoshi's vanguards at Komaki and Nagakute, but after Nobukatsu surrendered he submitted, and in 1586 became Hideyoshi's vassal.
sections.deeds:
After the campaign of 1590 against the Hōjō, Ieyasu gave up his five provinces and in 1591 moved his soldiers and vassals to eight provinces in the Kantō, with his seat at Edo, then an underdeveloped town. Modern Japanese historians note that the move was Hideyoshi's order; Andō Yūichirō sees it as having doubled his territory. In 1598 the dying Hideyoshi named him one of five regents for the child Toyotomi Hideyori, the most powerful of them. Opposition gathered around Ishida Mitsunari, and on 21 October 1600, Ieyasu's Eastern Army, initially 75,000 men, met a Western Army of 120,000 at Sekigahara. Ieyasu had for months promised land and leniency to western daimyo who changed sides, and the battle ended in an overwhelming victory.

He redistributed the domains: allies were enlarged, some western houses destroyed, and Hideyori reduced to an ordinary daimyo. On 24 March 1603, Emperor Go-Yōzei gave him the title of shōgun. He abdicated in 1605 in favour of his son Hidetada, showing that the office would be hereditary, but as retired shōgun at Sunpu remained the effective ruler. He supervised the building of Edo Castle, the largest in Japan, at the expense of the other daimyo, and accepted the rule that each lord maintain a residence in Edo.

In 1611 and 1612 the daimyo swore to his Three Laws. The Kuge shohatto of 1613 placed the court nobles under strict supervision, and the Buke shohatto of 1615 allowed each daimyo only one castle. He dealt with the Netherlands, Spain and England, often consulting the English pilot William Adams.
sections.opponents:
Ieyasu's enemies in war were the Imagawa, the Takeda, the Hōjō and finally the Toyotomi party; within his own house the Ikkō-ikki rising drew away some of his vassals, and Ishikawa Kazumasa defected to Hideyoshi in 1585. His conduct included acts recorded as atrocities. After taking Horikawa Castle in 1569 he ordered the prisoners and residents massacred, women and children among them; around 700 people are recorded as beheaded. In 1579, when Nobunaga accused Lady Tsukiyama and Nobuyasu of conspiring with Takeda Katsuyori, Ieyasu had his wife executed and forced his son to commit seppuku. The account in the Mikawa Monogatari is thought implausible by modern historians, and Katsuhiro Taniguchi prefers a theory of conflict between factions at Hamamatsu and Okazaki.

After the winter siege of Osaka in 1614 the Tokugawa filled in the castle's outer moats once an armistice was agreed, and attacked again. According to George Sansom he was cruel, relentless and merciless towards the Toyotomi survivors: for days scores of men and women were hunted down and executed, among them an eight-year-old son of Hideyori, who was beheaded. Hamada Koichiro records that historians after the Meiji Restoration portrayed him as a “cunning old man” who used a temple bell as a pretext for war. Watanabe Daimon, by contrast, stresses his readiness to forgive enemies and vassals who had betrayed him.

At first tolerant of Christianity, he turned against it after the Okamoto Daihachi incident of 1612 and in 1614 signed an edict banning the religion and expelling foreign missionaries.
sections.last:
The last threat to Ieyasu's rule was Toyotomi Hideyori, the son and heir of Hideyoshi, a young daimyo in Osaka Castle around whom samurai opposed to the Tokugawa gathered. Ieyasu found fault with the opening ceremony of a temple built by Hideyori, as though it prayed for his death and the ruin of his house, and ordered him to leave Osaka; those in the castle refused. In 1614 Ieyasu and the shōgun Hidetada besieged the castle. An armistice followed after cannon fire threatened Hideyori's mother, Yodo-dono. When Hideyori refused a further order to leave, Ieyasu attacked again with 155,000 soldiers. The castle fell in 1615 and nearly all its defenders were killed, including Hideyori, his mother and his infant son; Ieyasu refused the plea of Hideyori's wife Senhime, his own granddaughter, for their lives.

Ieyasu died in 1616 at the age of 73. The cause is thought to have been cancer or syphilis. His chief physician, Sotetsu Katayama, diagnosed stomach cancer, but Ieyasu took the illness for a tapeworm, refused the medicine prepared for him and kept to his own remedies, while his health declined; when his son Hidetada also warned him, he was angered, and he exiled the physician. He had wished to be deified after death to protect his descendants, and was given the name Tōshō Daigongen. His remains were buried at Kunōzan; many believe that they were reburied at Nikkō after the first anniversary of his death, but neither shrine has opened the graves. At his death his personal wealth was estimated at about 4 million koku, and he possessed about 42 tons of gold.
sections.legacy:
The Tokugawa shogunate, the third shogunal government after the Kamakura and the Ashikaga, ruled Japan for the next 260 years and opened the Edo period. Edo became the centre of political power and the de facto capital, though Kyoto remained the seat of the emperor; the Imperial Palace now stands on the site of Edo Castle. The system known as bakuhan used graded rewards and punishments to make the daimyo and samurai live in peace under the shogunate. The lords who had pledged themselves before Sekigahara became the fudai daimyō and those who did so afterwards the tozama, regarded as inferior. In 1639 his successors enacted the sakoku policy, which closed Japan to the outside world, with some exceptions, for over 200 years.

Ieyasu is counted the third of the three “Great Unifiers” of Japan, with Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi. His shrines at Kunōzan and Nikkō gave their name to the gongen style of architecture. A devotee of the Jōdo-shū school of Buddhism, he moved his family temple to Zōjō-ji in Edo and later patronised Confucian scholars such as Hayashi Razan.

Assessments differ. Junji Mitsunari traces his boldness to a childhood of hardship as a hostage; John T. Kuehn sees a master of long strategies; Kazuto Hongō credits him with stability built on the use of his vassals' abilities and on systems of succession rather than on single individuals. After the Meiji Restoration historians tended to present him as cunning. His life served as the model for Lord Toranaga in James Clavell's novel Shōgun.

summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543–1616) rose from hostage son of a minor daimyo to ally of Oda Nobunaga and leading vassal of Toyotomi Hideyoshi. Victory at Sekigahara in 1600 made him master of Japan, and as shōgun from 1603 he founded a government that lasted until 1868. He destroyed the Toyotomi line at Osaka in 1615.

notes: Dates are month-first in the article (January 31, 1543; June 1, 1616; October 21, 1600; March 24, 1603) and are kept so in facts and sections; events carry years only.
Father's death: the article says 1549 'when Takechiyo was six' and has him five at his abduction, held three years, then nine in 1551; ages left out except 'five-year-old'.

Break with the Imagawa: the article gives 1560 (reclaims Okazaki, secret alliance), 1561 (openly ends allegiance) and also 'In 1566, when Ieyasu declared his independence'; 1560 and 1561 used, 1566 left out. The Kiyosu Alliance is dated only 'sometime in the aftermath of Okehazama' under a 1562 heading.

Move to the Kantō: the article says 'In 1591, Ieyasu gave up control of his five provinces' but also that the proclamation was made the day Hideyoshi entered Odawara (the 1590 campaign); event dated 1591 as the article states, text mentions the 1590 campaign.

Submission to Hideyoshi: the article has Ieyasu 'decide to submit' after Nobukatsu's surrender and 'finally decide to become Hideyoshi's vassal' in 1586 after Hideyoshi sent his mother as hostage; 1586 used.

Fall of Osaka: the article says 'In late 1615, Osaka Castle fell' after the 'Summer Siege'; only the year is given here. It says Ieyasu 'either required them to commit seppuku, or killed both of them'; the text here says only that they died/were killed.
Sekigahara numbers: 75,000 and 120,000 'initially', then 'a total of 170,000'; first pair used.
The lede says he was the 'most senior officer' under the Toyotomi; the Kantō section says 'second most powerful daimyo'; neither phrase used.
Hidetada named heir in 1579 'since his second son had been adopted by Toyotomi Hideyoshi' looks anachronistic; left out. The lede's 'shifted the government to Edo in 1638' also left out.
The 1604 rule on Edo residences is said to be advice of Tōdō Takatora and Date Masamune that Ieyasu 'accepted and implemented'.
The 'temple bell' pretext (Hōkō-ji) appears in Hamada Koichiro's remarks; the Osaka section speaks only of the 'opening ceremony of a temple'.

The Family section of the saved article is headings only: numbers of wives and children are not available. The Okamoto Daihachi incident is dated 1612 in one section while Religion says the attitude changed 'after 1613'.
